options: Only phantom reads
Only dirty reads
All three: dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads
Only nonrepeatable reads and phantom reads, but not dirty reads
questions.explain: SERIALIZABLE is the strictest ANSI isolation level and the only one that prevents all three classic anomalies.

questions.q: What mechanism does SERIALIZABLE use to prevent phantom reads, that REPEATABLE READ doesn't have?
options: It uses row versioning instead of locks for everything
It disables INSERT statements globally while any transaction is open
Range locks, which lock the entire gap a predicate describes, not just existing matching rows
It takes an exclusive lock on the whole database
questions.explain: A range lock locks the whole span a predicate like 'BETWEEN 500 AND 1000' covers, so a new row that would fall in that range can't be inserted until the lock is released.

questions.q: In the phantom-read timeline, what happens to Session B's INSERT if Session A runs under SERIALIZABLE instead of REPEATABLE READ?
options: Session A's transaction automatically fails
Session B's INSERT still commits immediately, with no change
Session B's INSERT succeeds but is invisible to Session A
Session B's INSERT is blocked until Session A's transaction commits or rolls back
questions.explain: Because the new row's ListPrice falls inside the range Session A has locked, the INSERT must wait for Session A's transaction to finish.

questions.q: What is the main cost of SERIALIZABLE compared to the other ANSI isolation levels?
options: It silently returns incorrect results under heavy load
It cannot be used with SELECT statements
It causes the most blocking of any standard isolation level, including blocking entirely new inserts within a locked range
It uses significantly more disk space per transaction
questions.explain: Range locks can block not just updates to existing rows but new inserts falling within the locked predicate's range, making SERIALIZABLE the most blocking standard level.

questions.q: When is SERIALIZABLE actually worth its cost?
options: Only for SELECT statements that touch a single row
When specific business logic genuinely cannot tolerate a phantom row appearing or disappearing mid-transaction
For every single query in an application, as a safe default
Never -- it should always be avoided in favor of READ COMMITTED
questions.explain: SERIALIZABLE should be reserved for cases where a correctness requirement genuinely demands preventing phantoms -- for most code, a looser level is sufficient and costs less concurrency.
